title: Seeker of Goodness Who Seeks His Lord
intro: In Ighathat al-Lahfan, a work on the failings of the heart, Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya quotes a long poem without naming its author. Its editor, Muhammad Uzayr Shams, judges it to be Ibn al-Qayyim’s own. After challenging people who claim to follow the first Muslims, its closing verses picture the Prophet’s Companions walking among their neighbours and praying when everyone else is asleep. The poem finally puts the Qur’an into the listener’s hands, naming the passages in which to look for their likeness.

translation: Seeker of goodness who seeks his Lord,
hoping to gain from Him all he hopes for,
1.sharh: The listener wants to worship God well and hopes that God will grant his deepest wish. The address hangs in the air until the next verse gives him something to do.

translation: look to the example of the Companions
and the way they lived in days gone by.
2.sharh: The Prophet’s Companions are the men and women who knew him as believers. The seeker is asked to look at how they actually lived.

translation: Follow the road they took wherever they turned.
Keep right. The road does not lie to the left.
3.sharh: The seeker becomes a traveller at a fork in the road. In Arabic the right hand also carries associations of good fortune, giving the directions a moral force.

translation: By God, they chose for themselves only
the paths of guidance in word and deed.
4.sharh: The oath answers the traveller’s need to trust his guides. The road they chose could be traced in what they said as well as what they did.

translation: They walked in the Messenger’s footsteps and followed his example,
taking him as their model in every circumstance.
5.sharh: The Companions whom the listener follows were themselves followers. Their authority comes from the example of the Messenger that shaped their conduct in every part of life.

translation: What fine companions for a seeker of guidance.
His journey ends well when all are gathered.
6.sharh: By walking in their footsteps, someone born centuries later can still travel in their company. The journey ends at the gathering of the dead for judgement.

translation: Devout in their obedience, humble before their Lord,
speaking words of the utmost truth,
7.sharh: Two words describe the worshipper from within, obedience steadily maintained and a heart made humble. Speech gives that inward disposition an audible form.

translation: leaving every evil deed behind
and doing the best of deeds.
8.sharh: The repeated participles carry the list over from the previous verse. Restraint is only half the picture, since they also go looking for good they can do.

translation: Their desires follow the religion of their Prophet.
Others stand at the opposite extreme.
9.sharh: Desire has a place in this account, but it follows where faith leads. The unnamed opponents earlier in the poem are accused of reversing that order.

translation: No flaw tainted their faith, nor was there
in their speech the wild claim of an ignorant zealot.
10.sharh: The poet hears none of the extravagant pronouncements he criticised earlier in the poem. A speaker’s intensity of feeling, in that earlier dispute, was being offered as authority.

translation: They acted on what they knew and affected nothing.
So they never mixed guidance with error.
11.sharh: They keep within the bounds of what they know, and put that knowledge to work. The Arabic verbs for acting and knowing use the same three consonants in a different order.

translation: Others took the opposite course, to the point
of abandoning guidance and calling others astray.
12.sharh: The charge grows more serious across the break. Those under criticism first lose their own way and then actively call others to join them.

translation: They are guides for the bewildered. Whoever walks
by their guidance need not fear being led astray.
13.sharh: The bewildered traveller of the opening now has guides. The last word echoes the previous verse, turning the danger of being misled into something the traveller can leave behind.

translation: They are the stars in guidance and in light,
in loftiness of station and in being beyond reach.
14.sharh: A traveller can steer by a star and see by its light without ever drawing near it. The image holds together the help the Companions offer and the difficulty of attaining their rank.

translation: They walk gently among people. Their speech
is true, untouched by the folly of fools.
15.sharh: The gaze comes down from the stars to an ordinary street. The gentle walk recalls Qur’an 25:63, where the servants of the Merciful walk quietly and answer the foolish with peace.

translation: Forbearance and knowledge, with reverence and humility,
and goodwill joined to generosity.
16.sharh: The near rhyme of the Arabic words for forbearance and knowledge brings the two virtues together. In his discussion of the preceding Qur’anic image, Ibn al-Qayyim quotes al-Hasan al-Basri describing those who walk this way as learned and forbearing.

translation: They keep their night alive in obedience to their Lord,
reciting, pleading and asking.
17.sharh: Arabic calls a night spent awake in worship a night brought to life. Recitation gives way to the worshippers’ own entreaties and requests.

translation: Their eyes run over with tears
like the steady downpour of heavy rain.
18.sharh: The tears follow immediately on the night prayers. The poet chooses a sustained fall of heavy rain to give their private emotion weight and duration.

translation: Monks by night, and when they face
their enemy in battle, among the bravest champions.
19.sharh: “Monks” describes the intensity of their night vigil. The tenderness that drew tears in private belongs to the same people the poet pictures standing firm in public danger.

translation: When the race flag comes into view, you see them
vying with one another in good deeds.
20.sharh: The appearance of a race flag turns an invisible contest into something one can watch. Each competitor gains ground by doing good that benefits someone else.

translation: Their faces bear the trace of prostration before their Lord,
and on them shine rays of His light.
21.sharh: Prayer has left a recognisable expression on their faces. The image draws on the close of the chapter called Victory, which the very next verse names.

translation: The Book has indeed made their qualities plain to you
in the chapter of the clear and lofty victory.
22.sharh: The closing verse of the Qur’anic chapter Victory pictures Muhammad’s companions as merciful to one another and bowed in prayer, seeking God’s favour. The poem invites its listener to read the portrait there.

translation: The fourth of the seven long chapters describes them,
a people He loves, humble towards others.
23.sharh: Counting the long chapters from The Cow places The Table Spread fourth. In Qur’an 5:54 God loves these people and they love Him. Ibn al-Qayyim understands their lowliness towards fellow believers as the tenderness with which they treat them.

translation: Disavowal and The Gathering give their likeness too,
as do “Has There Come” and The Spoils.
24.sharh: Four more chapters send the listener back to acts of mutual care, migration and hospitality. “Has There Come” identifies The Human Being by its opening words.

1.1.2.head: باغٍ
1.1.2.meaning: One who seeks or desires something.

1.1.3.head: إِحسان
1.1.3.meaning: Ihsan is doing something well, here the excellence of a person’s worship.

2.1.3.head: هَدي
2.1.3.meaning: A manner of life which others may follow.

3.1.5.head: تَيَمَّمَ
3.1.5.meaning: To head for a particular place.

5.1.1.head: دَرَجَ
5.1.1.meaning: To walk on, to proceed along a path.

6.2.1.head: مَآل
6.2.1.meaning: The outcome, the place or state someone finally reaches.

6.2.3.head: حَشر
6.2.3.meaning: Hashr is the gathering of all people after resurrection for judgement.

7.1.2.head: مُخبِت
7.1.2.meaning: Humble before God and inwardly at rest.

9.2.3-5.meaning: “Of this condition.” The reciter says min, “of, from”. Both editions read fi, “in”.

10.1.2.head: شابَ
10.1.2.meaning: To mingle with, here to taint. The electronic Riyadh text reads “marred them”. The Egyptian printing of al-Fiqi has “tainted them”.

10.2.3.head: شَطح
10.2.3.meaning: An extravagant utterance, especially a claim made in a state of spiritual excitement.

11.2.3.head: شابَ
11.2.3.meaning: To mix one thing with another.

13.1.2.head: دَليل
13.1.2.meaning: A guide who shows someone the way. The plural here refers to people.

14.2.4.head: مَنال
14.2.4.meaning: Something within reach or within one’s power to attain.

15.1.4.head: هَون
15.1.4.meaning: Gentleness and composure in one’s gait.

16.1.1.head: حِلم
16.1.1.meaning: Forbearance, the ability to hold one’s temper.

16.2.4.head: إِفضال
16.2.4.meaning: Generosity in conferring a benefit on another.

17.1.1-2.head: أَحيا لَيلَهُ
17.1.1-2.meaning: “To bring one’s night to life” means spending it awake in worship.

18.2.3.head: وابِل
18.2.3.meaning: Heavy rain falling in large drops.

19.1.3.head: راهِب
19.1.3.meaning: A monk, here invoked for the time spent awake in prayer.

20.1.3-4.head: عَلَم الرِّهان
20.1.3-4.meaning: “The race flag” marks the course towards which the contestants run.

21.2.4.head: مُتَلالٍ
21.2.4.meaning: Gleaming or glittering. The poet lightens the word’s final consonants for the rhyme.

22.2.2-3.head: سورَة الفَتح
22.2.2-3.meaning: Al-Fath, Victory, is chapter 48 of the Qur’an. Its final verse describes the Prophet’s companions.

23.1.1-3.head: رابِع السَّبع الطِّوال
23.1.1-3.meaning: “The fourth of the seven long chapters” is The Table Spread, specifically Qur’an 5:54.

23.2.4.head: إِذلال
23.2.4.meaning: The lowliness or gentleness shown to fellow believers in Qur’an 5:54.

24.1.1.head: بَراءَة
24.1.1.meaning: Bara’a, Disavowal, is another name for chapter 9, Repentance.

24.1.2.head: الحَشر
24.1.2.meaning: Al-Hashr, The Gathering, praises the emigrants, their hosts and those who came after them in verses 8–10.

24.2.1-2.head: هَل أَتى
24.2.1-2.meaning: “Has there come” opens chapter 76, The Human Being. Verses 7–10 describe people giving food for God’s sake.

24.2.4.head: الأَنفال
24.2.4.meaning: Al-Anfal means spoils. Its closing verses recall believers who migrated and those who sheltered and helped them.
